subtopic: Mean Free Path and Pressure of an Ideal Gas
stem: Obtain the mean free path of nitrogen molecule at \( 0\ ^\circ \text{C} \) and 1.0 atm pressure. The molecular diameter of nitrogen is 324 pm (assume that the gas is ideal).
solution:
Given \( T = 0\ ^\circ \text{C} = 273 \text{ K} \), \( P = 1.0 \text{ atm} = 1.01 \times 10^{5} \text{ Pa} \) and \( d = 324 \text{ pm} = 324 \times 10^{-12} \text{ m} \).

For ideal gas \( PV = N k_{B} T \), \( \therefore \dfrac{N}{V} = \dfrac{P}{k_{B} T} \).

Using Eq. (3.6), mean free path

\( \lambda = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}\, \pi d^{2} \left( \dfrac{N}{V} \right)} = \dfrac{k_{B} T}{\sqrt{2}\, \pi d^{2} P} \)

\( = \dfrac{\left( 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \text{ J/K} \right)\left( 273 \text{ K} \right)}{\sqrt{2}\, \pi \left( 324 \times 10^{-12} \text{ m} \right)^{2} \left( 1.01 \times 10^{5} \text{ Pa} \right)} \)

\( = 0.8 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m} \)

Note that this is about 247 times molecular diameter.

subtopic: RMS Speed and Interpretation of Temperature
stem: At 300 K, what is the rms speed of Helium atom? [mass of He atom is 4u, \( 1u = 1.66 \times 10^{-27} \) kg; \( k_{B} = 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \) J/K]
solution:
Given \( T = 300 \text{ K} \), \( m = 4 \times 1.66 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg} \)

Average \( K.E. = \dfrac{1}{2} m \overline{\mathrm{v}^{2}} = \dfrac{3}{2} k_{B} T \)

\( \therefore \overline{\mathrm{v}^{2}} = \dfrac{3 k_{B} T}{m} = \dfrac{3 \times 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \times 300}{4 \times 1.66 \times 10^{-27}} \)

\( = 187.05 \times 10^{4} \text{ m}^{2}/\text{s}^{2} \)

\( \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{rms}} = \sqrt{\overline{\mathrm{v}^{2}}} = 13.68 \times 10^{2} \text{ m/s} = 1368 \text{ m/s} \)

subtopic: Spectral Distribution and Wien's Displacement Law
stem: Calculate the value of \( \lambda_{\max} \) for solar radiation assuming that surface temperature of Sun is 5800 K \( \left( b = 2.897 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m K} \right) \). In which part of the electromagnetic spectrum, does this value lie?
solution:
Given \( T = 5800 \text{ K} \) and \( b = 2.897 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m K} \).

Using Eq. (3.45),

\( \lambda_{\max} = \dfrac{2.897 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m K}}{5800 \text{ K}} \)

\( = 4.995 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m} = 4995\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}} \)

This value lies in the visible region of the electromagnetic spectrum.

subtopic: Perfect Blackbody and Emissivity
stem: Calculate the energy radiated in one minute by a blackbody of surface area 200 \( \text{cm}^{2} \) at \( 127\ ^\circ \text{C} \) \( \left( \sigma = 5.67 \times 10^{-8} \text{ J m}^{-2} \text{s}^{-1} \text{K}^{-4} \right) \).
solution:
Given

\( A = 200 \text{ cm}^{2} = 200 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}^{2} \),

\( T = 127\ ^\circ \text{C} = (127 + 273) \text{ K} = 400 \text{ K} \),

\( t = 1 \text{ min} = 60 \text{ s} \)

We know that energy radiated is given by

\( Q = \sigma A t T^{4} \)

\( = 5.67 \times 10^{-8} \times 200 \times 10^{-4} \times 60 \times (400)^{4} \)

\( = 5.67 \times 1.2 \times 256 \)

\( = 1742 \text{ J} \)

subtopic: Perfect Blackbody and Emissivity
stem: A 60 watt filament lamp loses all its energy by radiation from its surface. The emissivity of the surface is 0.5. The area of the surface is \( 5 \times 10^{-5} \text{ m}^{2} \). Find the temperature of the filament \( \left( \sigma = 5.67 \times 10^{-8} \text{ J m}^{-2} \text{s}^{-1} \text{K}^{-4} \right) \).
solution:
Given, \( e = 0.5 \), \( A = 5 \times 10^{-5} \text{ m}^{2} \), \( \dfrac{dQ}{dt} = 60 \text{ W} = 60 \text{ J s}^{-1} \)

We know that \( \dfrac{dQ}{dt} = e \sigma A T^{4} \)

\( \therefore 60 = 0.5 \times 5.67 \times 10^{-8} \times 5 \times 10^{-5} \times T^{4} \)

\( \therefore T^{4} = \dfrac{60 \times 10^{13}}{5.67 \times 2.5} \)

\( T^{4} = 4.23 \times 10^{13} \)

\( \therefore T = \left( 42.3 \times 10^{12} \right)^{\frac{1}{4}} \)

\( T = 2.55 \times 10^{3} = 2550 \text{ K} \)

subtopic: Perfect Blackbody and Emissivity
stem: Assuming that the temperature at the surface of the Sun is 6000 K, find out the size of a virtual star (in terms of the size of Sun) whose surface temperature is 3000 K and the power radiated by the virtual star is 25 times the power radiated by the Sun. Treat both, the Sun and virtual star as a blackbody.
solution:
Given,

\( T_{\mathrm{Sun}} = 6000 \text{ K} \), \( T_{\mathrm{star}} = 3000 \text{ K} \), \( P_{\mathrm{star}} = 25 \times P_{\mathrm{Sun}} \)

Power radiated by the Sun

\( = P_{\mathrm{Sun}} = \left( \dfrac{dQ}{dt} \right)_{\mathrm{Sun}} = \sigma A_{\mathrm{Sun}} T_{\mathrm{Sun}}^{4} = \sigma 4 \pi r_{\mathrm{Sun}}^{2} T_{\mathrm{Sun}}^{4} \)

Power radiated by the virtual star

\( = P_{\mathrm{star}} = \left( \dfrac{dQ}{dt} \right)_{\mathrm{star}} = \sigma A_{\mathrm{star}} T_{\mathrm{star}}^{4} = \sigma 4 \pi r_{\mathrm{star}}^{2} T_{\mathrm{star}}^{4} \)

\( \therefore \dfrac{P_{\mathrm{star}}}{P_{\mathrm{Sun}}} = \dfrac{\sigma 4 \pi r_{\mathrm{star}}^{2} T_{\mathrm{star}}^{4}}{\sigma 4 \pi r_{\mathrm{Sun}}^{2} T_{\mathrm{Sun}}^{4}} = \dfrac{r_{\mathrm{star}}^{2}\, 3000^{4}}{r_{\mathrm{Sun}}^{2}\, 6000^{4}} = 25 \)

\( \therefore \dfrac{r_{\mathrm{star}}^{2}}{r_{\mathrm{Sun}}^{2}} = 25 \times \dfrac{6000^{4}}{3000^{4}} = 400 \)

or, \( r_{\mathrm{star}} = 20 \times r_{\mathrm{Sun}} \)
